subject: Biology
title: Structural Organisation in Animals
summary: The rationalised chapter is short and almost entirely about one animal: the Indian bullfrog, Rana tigrina, as the representative vertebrate. After a page on how cells build tissues, organs and organ systems, NCERT describes the frog's habits, its external features (morphology) and then, system by system, its anatomy: digestive, respiratory, circulatory, excretory, nervous with sense organs, endocrine and reproductive. Nearly every question in the school final is a labelled diagram, a named structure with its function, or a precise NCERT fact (three-chambered heart, nucleated RBCs, ten pairs of cranial nerves, 2500 to 3000 ova), so the whole chapter can be prepared by drawing the four NCERT figures and learning the anatomy paragraph by paragraph.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper set by the school on the CBSE pattern. Structural Organisation in Animals belongs to Unit II, Structural Organisation in Plants and Animals, which carries 11 marks shared with Morphology of Flowering Plants and Anatomy of Flowering Plants. Because the rationalised chapter is now only the frog, it usually contributes about 3 to 5 marks in a school final: a 1-mark MCQ or Assertion–Reason on a fact (chambers of the heart, nucleated RBCs, ureotelic, copulatory pad), a 2-mark or 3-mark question on a system, and quite often a 5-mark question asking for the labelled digestive system or the male reproductive system with a description. In NEET the unit is a regular source of one or two questions, lifted almost word for word from the NCERT anatomy paragraphs; NEET also still lists animal tissues under this unit, which is why a background section on tissues is included at the end of this guide.

question_types.note: One-line NCERT facts: number of heart chambers, nucleated RBCs, ureotelic, location of the copulatory pad, number of vasa efferentia, Bidder's canal, mesorchium, number of cranial nerve pairs, number of ova laid, which respiratory organ works in water, which gland is or is not endocrine, the sperm route through the kidney, hepatic versus renal portal system.

Why the alimentary canal is short (carnivore); why the frog never drinks water (absorbs through skin); poikilotherm versus warm-blooded; hibernation and cutaneous respiration; sexual dimorphism and vocal sacs; ureter as urinogenital duct in the male; why the heart keeps beating outside the body.

Function of ureters in frog (NCERT exercise); aestivation versus hibernation; two differences between male and female frog; name the digestive glands and their secretions; define hepatic and renal portal systems; list the three parts of the brain with their lobes; name the sense organs; why is a frog called a poikilotherm.

Respiration in water and on land; structure of the heart with sinus venosus and conus arteriosus; the excretory system and why frog is ureotelic; the brain in three parts; path of sperm from testis to cloaca; blood and lymph of frog; economic and ecological importance of frogs.

Draw a neat labelled diagram of the digestive system of frog and describe digestion (the NCERT exercise, the most common 5-marker); describe the male and female reproductive systems with labelled diagrams; describe the morphology of the frog with a diagram; give an account of the circulatory system; describe control and coordination in frog (nervous system, endocrine glands, sense organs).

A passage on frogs during the monsoon (croaking, amplexus, external fertilisation, tadpole) or on a frog dissection or on aestivation and hibernation, followed by four sub-questions that test the same NCERT facts.

hot_topics: Digestive system of frog: labelled diagram (Figure 7.2) plus the sequence mouth to cloaca and the roles of liver, gall bladder, pancreas, bile and villi

Male and female reproductive systems: mesorchium, 10 to 12 vasa efferentia, Bidder's canal, urinogenital duct, ovaries with no connection to kidneys, 2500 to 3000 ova, external fertilisation, tadpole and metamorphosis
Circulatory system: three-chambered heart, sinus venosus, conus arteriosus, hepatic and renal portal systems, nucleated RBCs, lymph versus blood
Respiration: cutaneous in water; buccal cavity, skin and lungs on land; skin alone during aestivation and hibernation
Morphology and sexual dimorphism: head and trunk, no neck or tail, nictitating membrane, tympanum, four versus five digits, webbed feet, vocal sacs and copulatory pad in the male
Excretory system: bean-shaped kidneys, nephrons, ureters as urinogenital ducts in the male, urinary bladder ventral to rectum, ureotelic
Nervous system and sense organs: CNS, PNS and autonomic divisions, ten pairs of cranial nerves, fore-, mid- and hind-brain with their lobes, five kinds of sense organs
Habits of the frog: poikilotherm, camouflage (called mimicry in NCERT), aestivation and hibernation

sections.heading: Introduction and 7.1 Organ and Organ System
sections.body:
In a unicellular organism one cell does everything: it digests, respires, excretes and reproduces. A multicellular animal divides the same jobs among groups of cells. Even a simple animal like Hydra is built of several types of cells, with thousands of cells of each type; the human body has billions. The question NCERT asks is how these cells work together, and the answer is the hierarchy you have known since Class 9.

A tissue is a group of similar cells, along with the intercellular substances, that performs a specific function. NCERT makes a point you should quote: all complex animals are built from only four basic types of tissues, epithelial, connective, muscular and neural. Tissues are organised in a specific proportion and pattern to form an organ such as the stomach, lung, heart or kidney. Our heart, for example, contains all four types of tissue. When two or more organs perform a common function through their physical and/or chemical interaction they form an organ system, for example the digestive system or the respiratory system. Cells, tissues, organs and organ systems split up the work in a way that shows division of labour, and together they keep the whole body alive.

NCERT also observes that the complexity of organs and organ systems shows a discernible trend across the animal kingdom, which it calls the evolutionary trend (studied in Class 12). Two terms are then defined, and the definitions are asked as 1-mark and 2-mark questions. Morphology is the study of form, that is, of the externally visible features. For plants and microbes the term means only this; for animals it refers to the external appearance of the organs or parts of the body. Anatomy is conventionally used for the study of the morphology of the internal organs of animals. The chapter then applies both words to a single animal, the frog, which stands as the representative of the vertebrates.

formulas.expr: Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism
where: group of similar cells + intercellular substances with a specific function
tissues organised in a specific proportion and pattern (stomach, lung, heart, kidney)
two or more organs performing a common function by physical and/or chemical interaction

formulas.expr: Four basic animal tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, neural
where: the heart contains all four types

sections.tip: If asked to define morphology and anatomy, use NCERT's words: morphology is the study of externally visible features; anatomy is the study of the morphology of internal organs. Do not write 'anatomy is the study of the body'.

sections.heading: 7.2 Frogs: classification, habitat and the habits examiners ask about
sections.body:
Frogs live both on land and in freshwater. They belong to class Amphibia of phylum Chordata, and the most common species in India is Rana tigrina, the Indian bullfrog. Every fact in this short section turns up as a 1-mark question, so learn the exact words.

Cold-blooded. Frogs do not have a constant body temperature; their body temperature varies with the temperature of the environment. Such animals are called cold-blooded or poikilotherms. This is the reason a frog is sluggish in cold weather and why it has to escape extreme temperatures altogether rather than regulate them.

Colour change. A frog looks different in grass and on dry land. It can change its colour to hide from enemies; this is camouflage. NCERT then says that this protective coloration is called mimicry. Strictly, in ecology, mimicry means resembling another organism, but in this chapter you should reproduce the NCERT sentence as it stands, because the examiner's key follows the textbook.

Aestivation and hibernation. Frogs are not seen during peak summer or peak winter. During these periods they take shelter in deep burrows to protect themselves from extreme heat and cold. The summer sleep is aestivation; the winter sleep is hibernation. In both states the frog is inactive, its metabolism is low, the lungs are not used and all gaseous exchange takes place through the moist skin (this link with cutaneous respiration is a favourite 2-mark and Assertion–Reason question).

Keep the three habits together in one line for the exam: poikilotherm (temperature), camouflage or mimicry (colour), aestivation and hibernation (seasonal dormancy). Two-mark questions ask you to distinguish aestivation from hibernation; the only difference the examiner wants is summer versus winter, plus the fact that both are spent in burrows and both are survival responses to extreme temperature.

formulas.expr: Frog: Phylum Chordata, Class Amphibia; Indian species Rana tigrina
Poikilotherm = body temperature varies with environment (cold-blooded)
where: must escape extreme heat and cold by aestivation and hibernation

formulas.expr: Aestivation = summer sleep; Hibernation = winter sleep; both in deep burrows, gas exchange through skin

sections.tip: Write 'poikilotherm' with the exact spelling; many students lose the mark by writing 'poikilothermic animal has constant temperature'. It is the opposite: variable temperature.

sections.heading: 7.2.1 Morphology: external features and sexual dimorphism
sections.body:
This section is NCERT Figure 7.1 in words, and the labelled figure is worth drawing in a 3- or 5-mark answer.

Skin. The skin is smooth and slippery because of mucus and is always kept moist. The dorsal side is generally olive green with dark irregular spots; the ventral side is uniformly pale yellow. The frog never drinks water; it absorbs water through the skin. (The summary adds that the skin has mucous glands and is highly vascularised, which is what makes it a respiratory surface.)

Body divisions. The body is divisible into head and trunk only. A neck and tail are absent. This is a classic trap question: any option that gives the frog a neck or a tail is wrong.

Head. Above the mouth there is a pair of nostrils. The eyes are bulged and covered by a nictitating membrane that protects them while the frog is in water. On either side of the eyes is a membranous tympanum (ear) that receives sound signals; there is no external ear.

Limbs. The forelimbs and hind limbs help in swimming, walking, leaping and burrowing. The hind limbs end in five digits and are larger and more muscular than the forelimbs, which end in four digits. The feet have webbed digits that help in swimming. So the two numbers to remember are 4 (fore) and 5 (hind).

Sexual dimorphism. Frogs show sexual dimorphism, which means the male and female can be told apart externally. Male frogs are distinguished by (i) sound-producing vocal sacs and (ii) a copulatory pad on the first digit of the forelimbs. Both are absent in female frogs. The vocal sacs give the croaking call that attracts the female; the copulatory pad (nuptial pad) helps the male grip the female during amplexus, the mating clasp. NEET has asked the exact location of the copulatory pad more than once, and the answer is always the first digit of the forelimb, not the hind limb.

A typical 2-mark question asks for two differences between male and female frogs, and a 3-mark question asks you to describe the external features with a diagram. Draw a dorsal view: head with bulging eyes, nostrils and tympanum, the trunk, short forelimbs with four digits and long folded hind limbs with five webbed digits.

formulas.expr: Body = head + trunk; neck and tail absent
where: olive green with dark irregular spots

formulas.expr: Forelimb: 4 digits; Hind limb: 5 digits, larger and muscular, webbed for swimming
Male frog = vocal sacs + copulatory pad on first digit of forelimb; both absent in female
Eye covered by nictitating membrane; tympanum on either side of eyes receives sound

sections.tip: The frog absorbs water through its skin and never drinks; and the digits are 4 in front, 5 behind. These two lines alone answer several MCQs.

sections.heading: 7.2.2 Anatomy: the digestive system
sections.body:
The body cavity of the frog holds the digestive, circulatory, respiratory, nervous, excretory and reproductive systems, and NCERT Figure 7.2 shows the internal organs with the complete digestive system. This is the most-asked diagram of the chapter and the first NCERT exercise, so draw it until you can do it in four minutes.

Parts. The digestive system consists of the alimentary canal and the digestive glands. The alimentary canal is short because frogs are carnivores, so the length of the intestine is reduced (an animal eating protein-rich prey needs less length for digestion than a herbivore). The mouth opens into the buccal cavity, which leads through the pharynx to the oesophagus. The oesophagus is a short tube that opens into the stomach, which continues as the intestine, then the rectum, and finally opens outside through the cloaca. The digestive glands are the liver, which secretes bile that is stored in the gall bladder, and the pancreas, which produces pancreatic juice containing digestive enzymes.

Process. Food is captured by the bilobed tongue, which is muscular, attached in front and free behind so that it can be flicked out at an insect. In the stomach, digestion takes place by the action of HCl and gastric juices secreted by the stomach wall. The partially digested food, called chyme, passes from the stomach into the first part of the small intestine, the duodenum. The duodenum receives bile from the gall bladder and pancreatic juice from the pancreas through a common bile duct. Bile emulsifies fat; pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins. Final digestion takes place in the intestine. The digested food is absorbed by the numerous finger-like folds of the inner wall of the intestine called villi and microvilli, which increase the absorptive surface. The undigested solid waste moves into the rectum and passes out through the cloaca.

For a 5-mark answer the marking scheme typically gives 2 or 3 marks for the labelled diagram and the rest for the sequence of organs and the roles of the two glands, chyme, bile and villi. Write the organs as a chain with arrows: mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → duodenum → intestine → rectum → cloaca.

formulas.expr: Mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → duodenum (small intestine) → intestine → rectum → cloaca
where: frog is a carnivore; intestine reduced in length

formulas.expr: Digestive glands: liver (bile, stored in gall bladder) and pancreas (pancreatic juice with enzymes)
where: carries bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenum

formulas.expr: Stomach: HCl + gastric juices → chyme; bile emulsifies fat; pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins; absorption by villi and microvilli

sections.tip: Do not write that the tongue is 'forked' or 'sticky' as the main point; NCERT says 'bilobed tongue captures food'. And bile emulsifies fat, it does not digest it.

sections.heading: Respiratory system: cutaneous, buccal and pulmonary respiration
sections.body:
Frogs respire on land and in water by two different methods, and every question on this system is really asking which organ works where.

In water. The skin acts as the aquatic respiratory organ. This is cutaneous respiration. Dissolved oxygen in the water is exchanged through the skin by simple diffusion. The skin can do this because it is thin, always moist (mucus) and highly vascularised, so there is a short diffusion path between the water and the blood in the skin capillaries.

On land. Three organs work: the buccal cavity, the skin and the lungs. Respiration by the lungs is pulmonary respiration. The lungs are a pair of elongated, pink-coloured, sac-like structures present in the upper part of the trunk region (thorax). Air enters through the nostrils into the buccal cavity and from there into the lungs. (The frog has no ribs or diaphragm; it fills the lungs by lowering and raising the floor of the buccal cavity, a positive-pressure buccal pump. This mechanism is not in the rationalised text, so mention it only as an extra.) The moist lining of the buccal cavity also exchanges gases directly, which is buccal respiration.

During aestivation and hibernation. The frog is dormant in a burrow, the lungs are not ventilated, and gaseous exchange takes place through the skin alone. Because the metabolic rate is very low in these states, the small amount of oxygen taken in through the skin is enough.

A 3-mark question typically asks you to explain respiration in frog in water and on land; a 2-mark question asks for the difference between cutaneous and pulmonary respiration. Answer both in the same shape: organ, medium, mechanism. Cutaneous: skin, water (and land, and dormancy), diffusion of dissolved oxygen through the moist vascular skin. Pulmonary: lungs, land only, air drawn through nostrils into the buccal cavity and then the lungs.

formulas.expr: In water: skin only (cutaneous respiration, diffusion of dissolved O<sub>2</sub>)
On land: buccal cavity + skin + lungs (pulmonary respiration); air path nostrils → buccal cavity → lungs
where: pair of elongated, pink, sac-like structures in the upper trunk (thorax)

formulas.expr: Aestivation and hibernation: gaseous exchange through skin

sections.tip: If an MCQ asks which organ respires 'both in water and on land', the answer is the skin. The lungs work only on land.

sections.heading: Blood vascular system and lymphatic system
sections.body:
The vascular system of the frog is a well-developed closed type, and the frog also has a lymphatic system. The blood vascular system involves the heart, blood vessels and blood; the lymphatic system consists of lymph, lymph channels and lymph nodes.

Heart. The heart is a muscular structure in the upper part of the body cavity, covered by a membrane called the pericardium. It has three chambers: two atria and one ventricle. A triangular chamber called the sinus venosus joins the right atrium; it receives blood from the body through the major veins, the venae cavae. The ventricle opens into a sac-like conus arteriosus on the ventral side of the heart, which carries blood out to the arteries. So the chain is: venae cavae → sinus venosus → right atrium → ventricle → conus arteriosus → arteries. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and skin. Because there is a single ventricle, oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix partly; NCERT's summary calls it a closed system with single circulation.

Vessels and portal systems. Arteries carry blood from the heart to all parts of the body (arterial system). Veins collect blood from the body and return it to the heart (venous system). The frog has two special venous connections that are asked again and again. The hepatic portal system is the venous connection between the intestine and the liver: blood from the gut goes to the liver before reaching the heart. The renal portal system is the venous connection between the lower parts of the body and the kidneys: blood from the hind region passes through the kidneys before reaching the heart. A portal vein, by definition, begins in capillaries and ends in capillaries.

Blood. Blood is composed of plasma and cells. The cells are RBCs (erythrocytes), WBCs (leucocytes) and platelets. The frog's RBCs are nucleated and contain the red pigment haemoglobin. (Mammalian RBCs lose their nucleus; frog RBCs do not; this is the single most common MCQ from the chapter.) Blood carries nutrients, gases and water to the respective sites during circulation, which is driven by the pumping of the muscular heart.

Lymph. Lymph is different from blood: it lacks a few proteins and RBCs. A 3-mark question on the circulatory system should mention: closed type, three-chambered heart with sinus venosus and conus arteriosus, arterial and venous systems, the two portal systems, and nucleated RBCs. The heart of a frog is myogenic and auto-excitable, so it continues to beat for some time after being removed from the body; this is an NCERT Exemplar and NEET item.

formulas.expr: Heart: 3 chambers = 2 atria + 1 ventricle; pericardium; sinus venosus (triangular, joins right atrium, receives venae cavae); conus arteriosus (sac-like, ventral, from ventricle)
Hepatic portal system: intestine → liver; Renal portal system: lower body → kidney
where: starts in capillaries and ends in capillaries of another organ before reaching the heart

formulas.expr: Blood = plasma + RBC (nucleated, haemoglobin) + WBC + platelets; Lymph = blood minus RBCs and a few proteins
Closed vascular system; single circulation; heart myogenic and auto-excitable

sections.tip: Frog heart has three chambers, but sinus venosus and conus arteriosus are accessory chambers and are not counted among the three. Do not write 'five-chambered'.

sections.heading: Excretory system
sections.body:
Nitrogenous wastes are removed by a well-developed excretory system consisting of a pair of kidneys, ureters, cloaca and urinary bladder.

Kidneys. The kidneys are compact, dark red, bean-like structures situated a little posteriorly in the body cavity, one on each side of the vertebral column. Each kidney is composed of many structural and functional units called uriniferous tubules or nephrons. (Zoologically the frog kidney is a mesonephros, a term not needed for the school exam.)

Ducts, and the male–female difference. In the male frog two ureters emerge from the kidneys and act as urinogenital ducts, because they carry both urine and sperms, and they open into the cloaca. In the female, the ureters and the oviducts open separately into the cloaca; the ureters carry only urine. The thin-walled urinary bladder lies ventral to the rectum and also opens into the cloaca; urine collects in it before being voided. This is the answer to NCERT exercise 2 (function of ureters): they conduct urine from the kidneys to the cloaca, and in the male they also conduct sperms, hence the name urinogenital duct.

Nature of waste. The frog excretes urea and is therefore a ureotelic animal. Excretory wastes are carried by the blood into the kidney, where they are separated (filtered by the nephrons) and excreted. Tadpoles, which live in water, excrete mostly ammonia (ammonotelic); the switch to urea at metamorphosis is a classic link with the Class 11 chapter on excretion, and an examiner may use it in an Assertion–Reason.

For a 3-mark answer: name the four parts, describe the kidneys (position, shape, colour, nephrons), state the urinogenital arrangement in male and female, state the position of the bladder and say the frog is ureotelic. A neat labelled diagram of the male urinogenital system (Figure 7.3) covers both this section and the reproductive one.

formulas.expr: Excretory system = pair of kidneys + ureters + cloaca + urinary bladder
where: compact, dark red, bean-like, on both sides of vertebral column, slightly posterior

formulas.expr: Male: ureter = urinogenital duct (urine + sperms) → cloaca; Female: ureter and oviduct open separately into cloaca
Urinary bladder: thin-walled, ventral to rectum, opens into cloaca; Frog is ureotelic (excretes urea)

sections.tip: Ureotelic is the adult frog. If a question mentions the tadpole, it is ammonotelic. Read which stage the question is about.

sections.heading: Control and coordination: endocrine glands and the nervous system
sections.body:
NCERT says the system for control and coordination is highly evolved in the frog and includes both the neural system and the endocrine glands.

Endocrine glands. Chemical coordination is achieved by hormones secreted by the endocrine glands. The prominent endocrine glands of the frog are the pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads (eight names; a 2-mark question asks you to list them, and an MCQ asks which of a list is not one of them, where the wrong entries are usually liver, salivary gland or kidney).

Divisions of the nervous system. The nervous system is organised into (i) a central nervous system, the brain and the spinal cord; (ii) a peripheral nervous system, the cranial and spinal nerves; and (iii) an autonomic nervous system, sympathetic and parasympathetic. There are ten pairs of cranial nerves arising from the brain (mammals have twelve; the difference is a common MCQ).

Brain. The brain is enclosed in a bony structure called the brain box or cranium. It is divided into fore-brain, mid-brain and hind-brain. The fore-brain includes the olfactory lobes, the paired cerebral hemispheres and the unpaired diencephalon. The mid-brain is characterised by a pair of optic lobes. The hind-brain consists of the cerebellum and the medulla oblongata. The medulla oblongata passes out through the foramen magnum and continues as the spinal cord, which is enclosed in the vertebral column. Draw the brain in dorsal view as a row of structures from front to back: olfactory lobes, cerebral hemispheres, diencephalon (with the pineal body on top), optic lobes, cerebellum (a small transverse band), medulla oblongata, spinal cord.

A 3-mark question on the nervous system expects the three divisions with their components, the number of cranial nerves, and the three parts of the brain with their lobes. Note the two adjectives NCERT uses: paired cerebral hemispheres and unpaired diencephalon; examiners look for them.

formulas.expr: Endocrine glands of frog: pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals, gonads
Nervous system: CNS (brain + spinal cord); PNS (cranial + spinal nerves); ANS (sympathetic + parasympathetic); 10 pairs of cranial nerves
Brain: fore-brain (olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres, unpaired diencephalon); mid-brain (pair of optic lobes); hind-brain (cerebellum, medulla oblongata)
where: opening through which medulla continues as spinal cord

sections.tip: Ten pairs of cranial nerves in frog, twelve in humans. The frog cerebellum is small, so draw it as a narrow band, not as a large lobed structure.

sections.heading: Sense organs
sections.body:
The frog has five kinds of sense organs, each named with its structure in NCERT: organs of touch (sensory papillae), taste (taste buds), smell (nasal epithelium), vision (eyes) and hearing (tympanum with internal ears). Of these, only the eyes and the internal ears are well-organised structures; the rest are cellular aggregations around nerve endings. This last sentence is a frequent 1-mark question, so remember which two are organised organs.

Eyes. The eyes are a pair of spherical structures situated in the orbit of the skull. They are simple eyes, possessing only one unit each; contrast this with the compound eyes of insects, which are made of many ommatidia. From morphology, recall that the eyes bulge and are protected by the nictitating membrane in water.

Ears. An external ear is absent; only the tympanum can be seen from outside. The ear is an organ of hearing as well as balance (equilibrium). The tympanum receives sound signals and passes the vibrations to the internal ear.

Questions here are short: list the sense organs with the structure for each (3 marks), or a 2-mark question on why the eyes of a frog are called simple eyes, or on the two functions of the ear. Answer in the NCERT pattern, organ then structure then function.

formulas.expr: Touch: sensory papillae; Taste: taste buds; Smell: nasal epithelium; Vision: eyes; Hearing and balance: tympanum + internal ear
where: only eyes and internal ears; the rest are cellular aggregations around nerve endings

formulas.expr: Eyes: pair, spherical, in the orbit, simple (single unit), with nictitating membrane; external ear absent

sections.tip: Frog has a tympanum but no external ear (pinna). Do not label 'ear' on the outside of the frog; label 'tympanum'.

sections.heading: Reproductive system, fertilisation, development and the importance of frogs
sections.body:
Frogs have well-organised male and female reproductive systems, drawn in NCERT Figures 7.3 and 7.4. Both figures are asked as 5-mark diagram questions, and the male system is also the source of the well-known sperm-route MCQ.

Male. The male reproductive organs are a pair of yellowish, ovoid testes, found adhered to the upper part of the kidneys by a double fold of peritoneum called the mesorchium. From each testis arise 10 to 12 vasa efferentia. They enter the kidney on their side and open into Bidder's canal, which runs along the kidney. Bidder's canal finally communicates with the urinogenital duct (the ureter) that comes out of the kidney and opens into the cloaca. The cloaca is a small median chamber used to pass faecal matter, urine and sperms to the exterior. So the route of sperms is: testis → vasa efferentia → kidney → Bidder's canal → urinogenital duct → cloaca. Notice that the sperms travel through the kidney, which is why the male frog's ureter is called a urinogenital duct.

Female. The female organs are a pair of ovaries situated near the kidneys, but with no functional connection with the kidneys. A pair of oviducts arising from (near) the ovaries opens into the cloaca separately from the ureters. A mature female can lay 2500 to 3000 ova at a time. The eggs are released into the body cavity and collected by the funnels of the oviducts; the ova shown in Figure 7.4 are the black-and-white eggs that fill the ovary in the breeding season.

Fertilisation and development. During the monsoon the male clasps the female (amplexus) using the copulatory pads and both shed gametes into water, so fertilisation is external and takes place in water. Development involves a larval stage called the tadpole, which is aquatic, has a tail and gills and feeds on plant matter. The tadpole undergoes metamorphosis, controlled by thyroid hormone, to form the adult frog: the tail is resorbed, limbs and lungs develop and the animal becomes a carnivore.

Importance. Frogs are beneficial to mankind because they eat insects and thus protect crops. They maintain ecological balance as an important link in food chains and food webs. In some countries the muscular legs of the frog are used as food. A 2-mark question on the importance of frogs needs any two of these three points.

formulas.expr: Male: pair of yellowish ovoid testes attached to kidneys by mesorchium (double fold of peritoneum); 10–12 vasa efferentia → kidney → Bidder's canal → urinogenital duct → cloaca
Female: pair of ovaries near kidneys, no functional connection with kidneys; pair of oviducts open separately into cloaca; 2500–3000 ova at a time
Fertilisation external, in water; larva = tadpole; tadpole → metamorphosis → adult
Importance: eat insects (crop protection); link in food chain and food web; legs eaten as food in some countries

sections.tip: Mesorchium attaches the testes, not the ovaries. And the ovary has no duct of its own: the oviduct opens into the cloaca separately from the ureter, so the female has no urinogenital duct.

sections.heading: Background for NEET: the four animal tissues (removed from the rationalised CBSE chapter, still in the NEET syllabus)
sections.body:
The rationalised NCERT chapter mentions the four tissues only in its introduction and summary, and CBSE school exams follow the rationalised book. NEET, however, still lists 'animal tissues' under this unit, and the older NCERT text on them is the source of one question most years. This section is a compact reference; skip it if you are preparing only for the school exam.

Epithelial tissue is a sheet of closely packed cells with one free surface, resting on a basement membrane, with little intercellular matrix. Simple epithelium is one layer: squamous (flat cells; walls of blood vessels, air sacs of lungs, diffusion), cuboidal (cube-like; ducts of glands, tubular parts of nephrons, secretion and absorption; the brush border of the proximal convoluted tubule), columnar (tall; lining of stomach and intestine, secretion and absorption) and ciliated (cuboidal or columnar cells with cilia; bronchioles and fallopian tubes, moving particles or mucus). Glandular epithelium is unicellular (goblet cells) or multicellular (salivary gland); exocrine glands pour secretions through ducts, endocrine glands are ductless. Compound epithelium is many-layered and protective, with little role in secretion or absorption: dry surface of skin, moist lining of buccal cavity, pharynx, inner lining of ducts of salivary and pancreatic glands. Cells are held by junctions: tight junctions stop leakage across a tissue, adhering junctions cement neighbours together, gap junctions allow rapid transfer of ions and small molecules between cells.

Connective tissue is the most abundant and widely distributed tissue; except blood, its cells secrete fibres of the structural proteins collagen and elastin, plus a modified polysaccharide matrix. Loose connective tissue: areolar (beneath skin; fibroblasts, macrophages and mast cells) and adipose (fat storage). Dense regular: tendons (muscle to bone) and ligaments (bone to bone), with parallel fibres. Dense irregular: skin, with fibres in many directions. Specialised: cartilage (solid, pliable, resists compression; chondrocytes in lacunae; tips of long bones, nose, ear, vertebrae, between adjacent bones of the vertebral column), bone (hard, non-pliable calcium-rich matrix, osteocytes in lacunae; the bone marrow of some bones makes blood cells) and blood (fluid matrix, plasma, with RBC, WBC and platelets).

Muscle tissue: skeletal (striated, voluntary, multinucleate fibres bundled in fascicles), smooth (non-striated, spindle-shaped, uninucleate, involuntary; blood vessels, gut wall), cardiac (striated, involuntary, branched, joined by intercalated discs which allow the cells to contract as a unit). Neural tissue: neurons are the excitable cells; neuroglia make up more than half the volume of neural tissue in our body and support and protect neurons.

key_terms.definition: A group of similar cells along with intercellular substances that performs a specific function; all complex animals have only four basic types: epithelial, connective, muscular and neural.

Tissues organised in a specific proportion and pattern form an organ (stomach, heart, kidney); two or more organs performing a common function through physical and/or chemical interaction form an organ system (digestive, respiratory).
The study of form or externally visible features; in animals, the external appearance of the organs or parts of the body.
The term conventionally used for the study of the morphology of the internal organs of animals.
A cold-blooded animal whose body temperature varies with the temperature of the environment; the frog is one.
The frog's ability to change its colour to hide from enemies; NCERT calls this protective coloration mimicry.
Summer sleep: the frog shelters in a deep burrow during peak summer to escape extreme heat; gaseous exchange during this period is through the skin.
Winter sleep: the frog shelters in a deep burrow during peak winter to escape extreme cold; gaseous exchange is through the skin.
A transparent membrane covering the bulged eyes of the frog that protects them while the frog is in water.
The membranous ear on either side of the eyes that receives sound signals; frogs have no external ear.
External difference between the sexes; the male frog has sound-producing vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of the forelimbs, both absent in the female.
The thickened pad on the first digit of the forelimb of a male frog that helps it grip the female during amplexus.
Exchange of gases through the moist, vascular skin by diffusion; the only mode in water and during aestivation and hibernation.
Respiration by the lungs, a pair of elongated pink sac-like structures in the upper trunk; used only on land.
The partially digested food that passes from the stomach into the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine.
Numerous finger-like folds of the inner wall of the intestine that absorb digested food by increasing the surface area.
A triangular chamber joined to the right atrium of the frog's heart that receives blood from the major veins, the venae cavae.
A sac-like structure on the ventral side of the heart into which the ventricle opens; it leads blood into the arteries.
The special venous connection between the intestine and the liver, so that blood from the gut passes through the liver before reaching the heart.
The special venous connection between the lower parts of the body and the kidneys.
Excreting nitrogenous waste mainly as urea, as the adult frog does.
The structural and functional unit of the frog's kidney.
In the male frog, the ureter, which carries both urine and sperms from the kidney to the cloaca.
A small median chamber that receives the rectum, the urinogenital or urinary ducts and the oviducts and passes faecal matter, urine and gametes to the exterior through the cloacal aperture.
The double fold of peritoneum by which the testes are attached to the upper part of the kidneys.
A canal inside the kidney of the male frog into which the 10 to 12 vasa efferentia open; it communicates with the urinogenital duct.
The aquatic larval stage of the frog that hatches from the externally fertilised egg and undergoes metamorphosis to form the adult.

formula_sheet.name: Classification of frog
formula_sheet.expr: Phylum Chordata, Class Amphibia; common Indian species Rana tigrina (Indian bullfrog); lives on land and in freshwater
formula_sheet.note: Cold-blooded (poikilotherm); camouflage called mimicry in NCERT; aestivation in summer, hibernation in winter, both in deep burrows.

formula_sheet.name: External features
formula_sheet.expr: Skin smooth, slippery (mucus), moist; dorsal olive green with dark irregular spots, ventral uniformly pale yellow; body = head + trunk, neck and tail absent; pair of nostrils above mouth; bulged eyes with nictitating membrane; tympanum on either side of eyes
formula_sheet.note: Frog never drinks water; absorbs it through the skin.

formula_sheet.name: Limbs and digits
formula_sheet.expr: Forelimbs: 4 digits; hind limbs: 5 digits, larger and muscular; webbed digits for swimming; limbs used for swimming, walking, leaping, burrowing
formula_sheet.note: 4 in front, 5 behind is the MCQ.

formula_sheet.name: Sexual dimorphism
formula_sheet.expr: Male: vocal sacs (sound) + copulatory pad on first digit of forelimb; female: both absent
formula_sheet.note: Copulatory pad location = first digit of the forelimb (NEET).

formula_sheet.name: Digestive system
formula_sheet.expr: Mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → duodenum → intestine → rectum → cloaca; glands = liver (bile, stored in gall bladder) + pancreas (pancreatic juice)
formula_sheet.note: Canal short because frog is a carnivore. Bilobed tongue captures food. HCl + gastric juice → chyme; bile emulsifies fat; pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins; absorption by villi and microvilli. Bile and pancreatic juice reach the duodenum through a common bile duct.

formula_sheet.name: Respiration
formula_sheet.expr: Water: skin (cutaneous, diffusion). Land: buccal cavity + skin + lungs (pulmonary). Air path: nostrils → buccal cavity → lungs
formula_sheet.note: Lungs: a pair of elongated, pink, sac-like structures in the upper trunk (thorax). During aestivation and hibernation gas exchange is through the skin.

formula_sheet.name: Heart
formula_sheet.expr: 3 chambers: 2 atria + 1 ventricle; covered by pericardium; sinus venosus (triangular, joins right atrium, receives venae cavae); conus arteriosus (sac-like, ventral, from ventricle)
formula_sheet.note: Closed vascular system, single circulation; heart is myogenic and auto-excitable, so it beats for some time after removal from the body.

formula_sheet.name: Portal systems
formula_sheet.expr: Hepatic portal system: intestine ↔ liver; Renal portal system: lower parts of body ↔ kidney
formula_sheet.note: Both are special venous connections; a portal vein begins and ends in capillaries.

formula_sheet.name: Blood and lymph
formula_sheet.expr: Blood = plasma + RBC (nucleated, haemoglobin) + WBC + platelets; lymph lacks a few proteins and RBCs
formula_sheet.note: Lymphatic system = lymph, lymph channels, lymph nodes.

formula_sheet.name: Excretory system
formula_sheet.expr: Pair of kidneys (compact, dark red, bean-like, either side of vertebral column, slightly posterior) + ureters + cloaca + urinary bladder (thin-walled, ventral to rectum); unit = uriniferous tubule (nephron)
formula_sheet.note: Male: ureters act as urinogenital ducts; female: ureters and oviducts open separately into cloaca. Frog is ureotelic (urea).

formula_sheet.name: Endocrine glands (8)
formula_sheet.expr: Pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals, gonads
formula_sheet.note: Liver, kidney and salivary glands are not endocrine glands.

formula_sheet.name: Nervous system
formula_sheet.expr: CNS = brain + spinal cord; PNS = cranial + spinal nerves; ANS = sympathetic + parasympathetic; 10 pairs of cranial nerves; brain in cranium (brain box)
formula_sheet.note: Fore-brain: olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres, unpaired diencephalon. Mid-brain: pair of optic lobes. Hind-brain: cerebellum + medulla oblongata → foramen magnum → spinal cord in vertebral column.

formula_sheet.name: Sense organs (5)
formula_sheet.expr: Touch: sensory papillae; taste: taste buds; smell: nasal epithelium; vision: eyes; hearing: tympanum with internal ears
formula_sheet.note: Only eyes and internal ears are well-organised; the rest are cellular aggregations around nerve endings. Eyes are simple eyes (one unit), in the orbit. External ear absent; ear = hearing + balance.

formula_sheet.name: Male reproductive system
formula_sheet.expr: Pair of yellowish ovoid testes attached to upper part of kidneys by mesorchium (double fold of peritoneum); 10–12 vasa efferentia → kidney → Bidder's canal → urinogenital duct → cloaca
formula_sheet.note: Sperms pass through the kidney; hence 'urinogenital' duct. Cloaca passes faeces, urine and sperms out.

formula_sheet.name: Female reproductive system and development
formula_sheet.expr: Pair of ovaries near kidneys (no functional connection with kidneys); pair of oviducts open separately into cloaca; 2500–3000 ova laid at a time; external fertilisation in water; tadpole larva → metamorphosis → adult
formula_sheet.note: Development is external; the tadpole has a tail and gills and is herbivorous.

formula_sheet.name: Importance of frogs
formula_sheet.expr: Eat insects and protect crops; important link in food chains and food webs; muscular legs used as food in some countries
formula_sheet.note: Any two points for a 2-mark question.

diagrams.title: External features of frog (NCERT Figure 7.1)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a dorsal view of a squatting frog: a broad, blunt head merging directly into a stout trunk with no neck, and no tail. On the head draw two large bulging eyes, a pair of small nostrils above the mouth line in front, and a round tympanum just behind each eye. Draw short forelimbs bent forward, each ending in four digits, and long hind limbs folded in a Z shape beside the trunk, each ending in five digits with webbing drawn between them. Label: head, trunk, eye, nictitating membrane (as a line over the eye), nostril, tympanum, fore limb (4 digits), hind limb (5 digits), web. For a male, add the label 'copulatory pad' on the first digit of the forelimb.

diagrams.title: Internal organs of frog showing the complete digestive system (NCERT Figure 7.2)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw an outline of the frog's trunk opened ventrally. At the top draw the heart as a small triangle; below it a large lobed liver on the animal's right side of the page with the small round gall bladder tucked under it, and a pair of elongated sac-like lungs beside the heart. From the mouth region draw the short oesophagus running down into a curved sac-like stomach on the left, continuing into the coiled intestine which fills the middle, then into the wider straight rectum ending in the cloaca and the cloacal aperture at the bottom. Draw the pancreas as a thin irregular strip in the loop between stomach and duodenum. On the dorsal side draw two bean-shaped kidneys with finger-like fat bodies above them, a ureter running down from each kidney to the cloaca, and the thin-walled urinary bladder as a bilobed sac ventral to the rectum. Label every one of: heart, oesophagus, liver, gall bladder, lung, stomach, pancreas, intestine, rectum, fat bodies, kidney, ureter, urinary bladder, cloaca, cloacal aperture.

diagrams.title: Male reproductive (urinogenital) system of frog (NCERT Figure 7.3)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two elongated bean-shaped kidneys side by side with a thin adrenal gland as a pale strip on the ventral surface of each. Above the upper end of each kidney draw a small yellowish oval testis attached to the kidney by a thin double line (the mesorchium), and finger-like fat bodies rising above each testis. From each testis draw 10 to 12 fine vasa efferentia entering the kidney. Along the outer margin of each kidney draw the urinogenital duct running down and opening into the cloaca; show the rectum coming down between the two ducts into the cloaca, the urinary bladder as a bilobed sac ventral to the rectum, and the cloacal aperture at the bottom. Label: testis, mesorchium, vasa efferentia, fat bodies, kidney, adrenal gland, Bidder's canal (a line along the kidney), urinogenital duct, rectum, urinary bladder, cloaca, cloacal aperture.

diagrams.title: Female reproductive system of frog (NCERT Figure 7.4)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a pair of large lobed ovaries filled with small circles for the ova, lying near but not attached to the kidneys. On each side draw a long, coiled, thick oviduct beginning as a funnel near the lungs, running down the side of the body cavity and opening into the cloaca separately. Draw the ureters coming from the kidneys and also opening into the cloaca, the rectum in the middle, the urinary bladder ventral to it, and the cloacal aperture. Label: ovary, ova, oviduct, kidney, ureter, urinary bladder, cloaca, cloacal aperture. Add the note 'ovaries have no functional connection with the kidneys; oviducts open separately into the cloaca'.

diagrams.title: Heart of frog in ventral view
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a conical ventricle pointing downwards with two atria as rounded chambers above it (the right atrium slightly larger). From the ventricle draw the sac-like conus arteriosus arising on the ventral surface and running upward and to the left, dividing into the two aortic trunks. Behind the atria draw the triangular sinus venosus (as a dotted outline, since it is dorsal) with the two anterior venae cavae and the posterior vena cava entering it. Show the pericardium as an outer dotted membrane. Label: right atrium, left atrium, ventricle, conus arteriosus, sinus venosus, vena cava, pulmonary veins entering left atrium, pericardium. Write beneath it: three chambers = two atria + one ventricle.

diagrams.title: Brain of frog in dorsal view
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a row of structures from front to back along a vertical axis. At the front two small oval olfactory lobes fused in the midline with olfactory nerves leaving forward; behind them two elongated cerebral hemispheres; then the narrow unpaired diencephalon with the pineal body drawn as a small stalked knob on top; then two large rounded optic lobes side by side; then the cerebellum as a thin transverse band; then the tapering medulla oblongata continuing as the spinal cord. Bracket the three regions and label: fore-brain (olfactory lobes, cerebral hemispheres, diencephalon), mid-brain (optic lobes), hind-brain (cerebellum, medulla oblongata), spinal cord.

diagrams.title: Respiratory organs of frog
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the head and anterior trunk of the frog in side view. Show the external nostrils leading through the internal nares into the buccal cavity, the glottis at the back of the buccal floor, and from it a short laryngotracheal chamber opening into a pair of elongated pink sac-like lungs in the upper trunk. Show the skin as a thick line and draw small capillaries under it. Label: external nostril, buccal cavity (buccal respiration), glottis, lung (pulmonary respiration), skin with blood capillaries (cutaneous respiration). Under the figure write: in water, skin only; on land, buccal cavity, skin and lungs; in aestivation and hibernation, skin only.

diagrams.title: Scheme of blood circulation showing the two portal systems
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the heart as a box in the centre with the sinus venosus feeding the right atrium and the conus arteriosus leaving the ventricle. Draw arteries (in one colour) leaving the conus to the head, the lungs and skin, the gut and the hind region. Draw veins returning to the sinus venosus through the venae cavae. Between the gut and the liver draw a vein labelled hepatic portal vein entering the liver, and from the liver a hepatic vein to the posterior vena cava. Between the hind limbs and the kidneys draw a vein labelled renal portal vein entering the kidney, and from the kidney renal veins joining the posterior vena cava. Add the pulmonary veins returning to the left atrium. Label: sinus venosus, right atrium, left atrium, ventricle, conus arteriosus, hepatic portal system (intestine to liver), renal portal system (lower body to kidney), vena cava, pulmonary vein.

ncert_questions.q: Draw a neat diagram of digestive system of frog.
ncert_questions.a: Draw NCERT Figure 7.2 as described in the diagrams section: heart at the top, liver with the gall bladder, the lungs, the oesophagus running into the stomach, the coiled intestine, the rectum ending in the cloaca and cloacal aperture, the pancreas between the stomach and the duodenum, and behind them the kidneys with fat bodies, ureters and the urinary bladder. Label at least: mouth/oesophagus, liver, gall bladder, stomach, pancreas, duodenum, intestine, rectum, cloaca, cloacal aperture. Under the figure add two lines the examiner rewards: the alimentary canal is short because the frog is a carnivore; the digestive glands are the liver (bile, stored in the gall bladder) and the pancreas (pancreatic juice).

ncert_questions.q: Mention the function of the ureters in frog.
ncert_questions.a: The ureters are a pair of ducts that emerge from the kidneys and open into the cloaca. They conduct urine from the kidneys to the cloaca. In the male frog the ureters also carry sperms, because the vasa efferentia enter the kidney and open into Bidder's canal, which communicates with the ureter; hence in the male the ureter acts as a urinogenital duct. In the female the ureters carry only urine and open into the cloaca separately from the oviducts.

ncert_questions.q: Frog's heart when taken out of the body continues to beat for some time. Select the best option from the following statements. (1) Frog is a poikilotherm. (2) Frog does not have any coronary circulation. (3) Heart is myogenic in nature. (4) Heart is autoexcitable. Options: (a) only (4); (b) (1) and (2); (c) (3) and (4); (d) only (3).
ncert_questions.a: Answer: (c) (3) and (4). The heart of the frog is myogenic, which means the impulse for contraction originates in the cardiac muscle itself, and it is auto-excitable, so it does not need nervous stimulation to beat. That is why an excised heart kept in a suitable saline continues to beat for some time. Poikilothermy and coronary circulation have nothing to do with it.

ncert_questions.q: Why is the alimentary canal of the frog short? Name the parts of the alimentary canal in sequence.
ncert_questions.a: The alimentary canal is short because frogs are carnivores; animal food is digested easily, so the length of the intestine is reduced. Sequence: mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → intestine (duodenum first, then the rest of the small intestine) → rectum → cloaca, which opens outside through the cloacal aperture.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the process of digestion in frog from the capture of food to absorption.
ncert_questions.a: Food (mostly insects) is captured by the bilobed tongue and passed through the buccal cavity, pharynx and oesophagus into the stomach. In the stomach, HCl and gastric juices secreted by the stomach wall partially digest the food into chyme. Chyme passes into the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine, which receives bile from the gall bladder and pancreatic juice from the pancreas through the common bile duct. Bile emulsifies fat; pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins. Final digestion takes place in the intestine. The digested food is absorbed by the finger-like folds of the intestinal wall, the villi and microvilli. Undigested solid waste moves into the rectum and is passed out through the cloaca.

ncert_questions.q: How does a frog respire in water and on land? What happens during aestivation and hibernation?
ncert_questions.a: In water the skin acts as the aquatic respiratory organ (cutaneous respiration): dissolved oxygen is exchanged through the moist, vascular skin by diffusion. On land the buccal cavity, the skin and the lungs act as respiratory organs; respiration by the lungs is pulmonary respiration. The lungs are a pair of elongated, pink, sac-like structures in the upper trunk; air enters through the nostrils into the buccal cavity and then into the lungs. During aestivation and hibernation the frog lies inactive in a burrow and gaseous exchange takes place through the skin only.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the structure of the heart of frog. Name the two portal systems of frog.
ncert_questions.a: The heart is a muscular organ in the upper part of the body cavity, covered by the pericardium. It has three chambers: two atria and one ventricle. A triangular sinus venosus joins the right atrium and receives blood from the major veins, the venae cavae. The ventricle opens into a sac-like conus arteriosus on the ventral side, which leads blood into the arteries. The two portal systems are the hepatic portal system, a venous connection between the intestine and the liver, and the renal portal system, a venous connection between the lower parts of the body and the kidneys.

ncert_questions.q: What are the cellular components of the blood of frog? How is lymph different from blood?
ncert_questions.a: Blood is composed of plasma and blood cells. The cells are RBCs (erythrocytes), which are nucleated and contain the red pigment haemoglobin; WBCs (leucocytes); and platelets. Lymph is different from blood in that it lacks a few proteins and RBCs. The lymphatic system consists of lymph, lymph channels and lymph nodes.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the excretory system of frog. Why is the frog called ureotelic?
ncert_questions.a: The excretory system consists of a pair of kidneys, ureters, cloaca and urinary bladder. The kidneys are compact, dark red, bean-like structures lying a little posteriorly in the body cavity on either side of the vertebral column; each is made of many uriniferous tubules (nephrons). In the male two ureters emerge from the kidneys and act as urinogenital ducts opening into the cloaca; in the female the ureters and the oviducts open separately into the cloaca. The thin-walled urinary bladder lies ventral to the rectum and opens into the cloaca. Blood carries the nitrogenous waste to the kidneys, where it is separated and excreted. The frog excretes urea, and is therefore called ureotelic.

ncert_questions.q: Give an account of the nervous system of frog.
ncert_questions.a: The nervous system is organised into (i) the central nervous system, consisting of the brain and spinal cord; (ii) the peripheral nervous system, consisting of cranial and spinal nerves, with ten pairs of cranial nerves arising from the brain; and (iii) the autonomic nervous system, sympathetic and parasympathetic. The brain is enclosed in the bony cranium (brain box) and has three parts. The fore-brain has the olfactory lobes, the paired cerebral hemispheres and the unpaired diencephalon. The mid-brain has a pair of optic lobes. The hind-brain has the cerebellum and the medulla oblongata. The medulla passes out through the foramen magnum and continues as the spinal cord, enclosed in the vertebral column.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the male reproductive system of frog with a labelled diagram. Trace the path of sperms from the testis to the exterior.
ncert_questions.a: Draw NCERT Figure 7.3 (see the diagrams section). The male reproductive organs are a pair of yellowish, ovoid testes attached to the upper part of the kidneys by a double fold of peritoneum called the mesorchium. From each testis arise 10 to 12 vasa efferentia, which enter the kidney on that side and open into Bidder's canal. Bidder's canal communicates with the urinogenital duct (the ureter), which comes out of the kidney and opens into the cloaca. The cloaca is a small median chamber that passes faecal matter, urine and sperms to the exterior through the cloacal aperture. Path of sperms: testis → vasa efferentia → kidney → Bidder's canal → urinogenital duct → cloaca → exterior.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the female reproductive system of frog. How do fertilisation and development take place?
ncert_questions.a: The female reproductive organs are a pair of ovaries situated near the kidneys, with no functional connection with the kidneys. A pair of oviducts arising near the ovaries opens into the cloaca separately from the ureters. A mature female lays 2500 to 3000 ova at a time. Fertilisation is external and takes place in water: during amplexus the male grips the female with the copulatory pads and both shed gametes into the water. Development is also external and involves a larval stage, the tadpole, which undergoes metamorphosis to form the adult frog.

ncert_questions.q: Name the sense organs of frog with the structure responsible for each. Which of them are well-organised organs?
ncert_questions.a: Touch: sensory papillae; taste: taste buds; smell: nasal epithelium; vision: eyes; hearing: tympanum with internal ears. Of these, only the eyes and the internal ears are well-organised structures; the rest are cellular aggregations around nerve endings. The eyes are simple eyes (one unit each) situated in the orbit; there is no external ear, only the tympanum is visible outside, and the ear serves both hearing and balance.

ncert_questions.q: Name the endocrine glands of frog. How does the male frog differ externally from the female?
ncert_questions.a: Endocrine glands: pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads. The male frog has sound-producing vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of each forelimb; both are absent in the female. This external difference is called sexual dimorphism.

ncert_questions.q: How are frogs beneficial to mankind?
ncert_questions.a: (i) Frogs eat insects and thus protect crops. (ii) They maintain ecological balance as an important link in food chains and food webs. (iii) In some countries the muscular legs of frogs are used as food by man.

pyq.q: The copulatory pad of a male frog is present on the
options: first digit of the hind limb
first digit of the fore limb
all digits of the fore limb
