pyq.solution: Male frogs have a copulatory pad on the first digit of the fore limbs (and vocal sacs); both are absent in females. Asked in NEET as well.

pyq.q: The RBCs of frog are
options: absent, oxygen is carried by plasma
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: NCERT: RBCs of frog are nucleated and contain the red pigment haemoglobin. Only mammalian RBCs are enucleated.

pyq.q: The heart of frog has
options: two chambers: one atrium and one ventricle
three chambers: two atria and one ventricle
three chambers: one atrium and two ventricles
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Two atria and one ventricle; sinus venosus and conus arteriosus are accessory chambers, not counted.

pyq.q: Select the correct route for the passage of sperms in a male frog.
options: Testes → vasa efferentia → Bidder's canal → ureter → cloaca
Testes → vasa efferentia → kidney → Bidder's canal → urinogenital duct → cloaca
Testes → Bidder's canal → kidney → vasa efferentia → urinogenital duct → cloaca
Testes → vasa efferentia → kidney → seminal vesicle → cloaca
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The vasa efferentia enter the kidney and open into Bidder's canal, which communicates with the urinogenital duct that opens into the cloaca. This exact question appeared in NEET 2017.

pyq.q: The renal portal system of frog is a special venous connection between the
options: kidney and the lower parts of the body
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Renal portal system: lower parts of the body to the kidney. The liver–intestine connection is the hepatic portal system.

pyq.q: The adult frog excretes mainly urea and is therefore
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Urea-excreting animals are ureotelic. The aquatic tadpole is ammonotelic.

pyq.q: The double fold of peritoneum that attaches the testes of a frog to the kidneys is the
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: NCERT: the testes adhere to the upper part of the kidneys by a double fold of peritoneum called mesorchium.

pyq.q: Which of the following is NOT an endocrine gland of frog?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: NCERT lists pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads. The liver is a digestive gland.

pyq.q: The number of pairs of cranial nerves arising from the brain of a frog is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Frog has ten pairs of cranial nerves; humans have twelve pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

pyq.q: Summer sleep of frog is called
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Aestivation is summer sleep; hibernation is winter sleep. Both are spent in deep burrows.

pyq.q: Which structure receives blood from the venae cavae in the frog's heart?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The triangular sinus venosus joins the right atrium and receives blood through the major veins called venae cavae. The conus arteriosus carries blood out of the ventricle.

pyq.q: In water, the frog respires through its
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: In water the skin is the only respiratory organ (cutaneous respiration). On land the buccal cavity, skin and lungs all work.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The alimentary canal of frog is short. Reason (R): Frogs are carnivores, so the length of the intestine is reduced.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: NCERT states the canal is short because frogs are carnivores and hence the intestine is reduced in length. R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): During hibernation, gaseous exchange in frog takes place through the skin. Reason (R): The skin of frog is moist and highly vascularised.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: In the burrow the lungs are not used; the moist, blood-rich skin allows diffusion of gases, which is why cutaneous respiration is possible. R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The RBCs of frog are nucleated. Reason (R): The blood of frog lacks haemoglobin.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Frog RBCs are nucleated (A true), and they contain the red pigment haemoglobin, so R is false.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The body of a frog has a distinct neck and a tail. Reason (R): The body of a frog is divisible into head and trunk.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Neck and tail are absent in the adult frog (A false); the body is divisible into head and trunk only (R true).

pyq.q: Assertion (A): In the male frog the ureter acts as a urinogenital duct. Reason (R): The vasa efferentia enter the kidney and open into Bidder's canal, which communicates with the ureter.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Because sperms pass through the kidney into the ureter, the ureter carries both urine and sperms; R is exactly why A is true.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Frogs are called cold-blooded animals. Reason (R): Frogs maintain a constant low body temperature.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Frogs are cold-blooded or poikilotherms (A true), but this means the body temperature varies with the environment, not that it is constant (R false).

pyq.q: Distinguish between aestivation and hibernation in frog.
pyq.answer: Aestivation is the summer sleep: during peak summer the frog shelters in a deep burrow to protect itself from extreme heat. Hibernation is the winter sleep: during peak winter it shelters in a deep burrow to escape extreme cold. In both states the frog is inactive with a very low metabolic rate, and gaseous exchange takes place through the skin.

pyq.q: How can a male frog be distinguished from a female frog?
pyq.answer: The male frog has (i) sound-producing vocal sacs and (ii) a copulatory pad on the first digit of each forelimb. Both are absent in the female. This external difference between the sexes is called sexual dimorphism.

pyq.q: Name the digestive glands of frog and state the function of their secretions.
pyq.answer: Liver: secretes bile, which is stored in the gall bladder; bile emulsifies fat. Pancreas: produces pancreatic juice containing digestive enzymes that digest carbohydrates and proteins. Both secretions reach the duodenum through the common bile duct.

pyq.q: What are the hepatic portal and renal portal systems of frog?
pyq.answer: The hepatic portal system is the special venous connection between the intestine and the liver, so that blood from the intestine passes through the liver before reaching the heart. The renal portal system is the special venous connection between the lower parts of the body and the kidneys.

pyq.q: Why does the frog never drink water? Why are frogs called poikilotherms?
pyq.answer: The frog never drinks water because it absorbs water through its moist, permeable skin. Frogs are called poikilotherms (cold-blooded) because they do not have a constant body temperature; their body temperature varies with the temperature of the environment.

pyq.q: Name the three parts of the brain of frog and the structures present in each.
pyq.answer: Fore-brain: olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres and unpaired diencephalon. Mid-brain: a pair of optic lobes. Hind-brain: cerebellum and medulla oblongata, which continues through the foramen magnum as the spinal cord.

pyq.q: Explain respiration in frog in water and on land. Name the respiratory organs in each case.
pyq.answer: In water: the skin is the aquatic respiratory organ (cutaneous respiration). Dissolved oxygen in the water is exchanged through the moist, vascular skin by diffusion. On land: the buccal cavity, skin and lungs act as respiratory organs; respiration by the lungs is pulmonary respiration. The lungs are a pair of elongated, pink, sac-like structures in the upper part of the trunk. Air enters through the nostrils into the buccal cavity and then into the lungs. During aestivation and hibernation gaseous exchange takes place through the skin only.

pyq.q: Describe the blood vascular system of frog.
pyq.answer: The vascular system is a well-developed closed type consisting of the heart, blood vessels and blood. The heart, covered by the pericardium, has three chambers, two atria and one ventricle; the triangular sinus venosus joins the right atrium and receives blood from the venae cavae, and the ventricle opens into the sac-like conus arteriosus on the ventral side. Arteries carry blood from the heart to all parts of the body and veins bring it back; two special venous connections exist, the hepatic portal system (intestine to liver) and the renal portal system (lower body to kidney). Blood consists of plasma and cells: nucleated RBCs with haemoglobin, WBCs and platelets. Circulation is single and is driven by the pumping of the muscular heart.

pyq.q: Describe the excretory system of frog. How does it differ in male and female frogs?
pyq.answer: The excretory system consists of a pair of kidneys, ureters, cloaca and urinary bladder. The kidneys are compact, dark red, bean-like structures lying a little posteriorly on either side of the vertebral column, each made of many nephrons (uriniferous tubules). The thin-walled urinary bladder lies ventral to the rectum and opens into the cloaca. The frog excretes urea (ureotelic). Difference: in the male the two ureters carry both urine and sperms and act as urinogenital ducts opening into the cloaca; in the female the ureters carry only urine and open into the cloaca separately from the oviducts.

pyq.q: Give an account of the control and coordination system of frog.
pyq.answer: Control and coordination involve the neural system and the endocrine glands. (i) Chemical coordination is by hormones from the endocrine glands: pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads. (ii) The nervous system has a central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), a peripheral nervous system (ten pairs of cranial nerves and the spinal nerves) and an autonomic nervous system (sympathetic and parasympathetic). (iii) The brain, enclosed in the cranium, has a fore-brain (olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres, unpaired diencephalon), a mid-brain (pair of optic lobes) and a hind-brain (cerebellum, medulla oblongata); the medulla continues through the foramen magnum as the spinal cord in the vertebral column.

pyq.q: Describe the external features of the head of a frog. What is the function of the nictitating membrane and the tympanum?
pyq.answer: The head is broad and merges with the trunk without a neck. A pair of nostrils lies above the mouth. The eyes are bulged and each is covered by a nictitating membrane, a transparent fold that protects the eye while the frog is in water. On either side of the eyes is a membranous tympanum (ear drum) that receives sound signals and transmits the vibrations to the internal ear; an external ear is absent. The mouth is wide and contains the bilobed tongue used to capture food.

pyq.q: Draw a neat labelled diagram of the digestive system of frog and describe the process of digestion.
pyq.answer:
Diagram (2 or 3 marks): NCERT Figure 7.2 with labels mouth/oesophagus, liver, gall bladder, stomach, pancreas, duodenum, intestine, rectum, cloaca, cloacal aperture (see the diagrams section for how to draw it).

Description: The digestive system consists of the alimentary canal and the digestive glands. The canal is short because frogs are carnivores. The mouth opens into the buccal cavity, which leads through the pharynx to the short oesophagus, then the stomach, the intestine, the rectum and the cloaca. The liver secretes bile, stored in the gall bladder; the pancreas secretes pancreatic juice with digestive enzymes. Food is captured by the bilobed tongue. In the stomach, HCl and gastric juices partially digest the food into chyme, which passes into the duodenum. The duodenum receives bile and pancreatic juice through the common bile duct: bile emulsifies fat and pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins. Final digestion occurs in the intestine and the digested food is absorbed by the villi and microvilli of the intestinal wall. Undigested solid waste passes through the rectum and out of the cloaca.

pyq.q: Describe the male and female reproductive systems of frog with labelled diagrams. Mention how fertilisation and development take place.
pyq.answer:
Male (draw Figure 7.3): a pair of yellowish ovoid testes attached to the upper part of the kidneys by the mesorchium, a double fold of peritoneum. 10 to 12 vasa efferentia from each testis enter the kidney and open into Bidder's canal, which communicates with the urinogenital duct that leaves the kidney and opens into the cloaca. The cloaca passes faeces, urine and sperms to the exterior. Labels: testis, mesorchium, vasa efferentia, kidney, adrenal gland, Bidder's canal, urinogenital duct, fat bodies, rectum, urinary bladder, cloaca, cloacal aperture.

Female (draw Figure 7.4): a pair of ovaries near the kidneys, with no functional connection with the kidneys, and a pair of coiled oviducts opening into the cloaca separately from the ureters. Labels: ovary, ova, oviduct, kidney, ureter, urinary bladder, cloaca, cloacal aperture. A mature female lays 2500 to 3000 ova at a time.

Fertilisation and development: fertilisation is external and takes place in water. Development involves a larval stage, the tadpole, which undergoes metamorphosis to form the adult.

pyq.q: Describe the morphology of frog with a labelled diagram, including the features that distinguish the male from the female.
pyq.answer:
Diagram: Figure 7.1, dorsal view, labelled head, trunk, eye, nostril, tympanum, fore limb, hind limb, webbed digits.

Skin: smooth, slippery due to mucus, always moist; dorsal side olive green with dark irregular spots, ventral side uniformly pale yellow; the frog never drinks water but absorbs it through the skin. Body: divisible into head and trunk; neck and tail absent. Head: a pair of nostrils above the mouth; bulged eyes covered by a nictitating membrane that protects them in water; a membranous tympanum on either side of the eyes that receives sound. Limbs: forelimbs and hind limbs help in swimming, walking, leaping and burrowing; the hind limbs end in five digits and are larger and more muscular than the forelimbs, which end in four digits; the feet have webbed digits for swimming. Sexual dimorphism: the male has sound-producing vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of the forelimbs, both absent in the female.

pyq.q: Give an account of the circulatory, respiratory and excretory systems of frog in brief.
pyq.answer:
Circulatory: closed vascular system with a lymphatic system. Three-chambered heart (two atria, one ventricle) in the pericardium; sinus venosus joins the right atrium and receives the venae cavae; the ventricle opens into the conus arteriosus on the ventral side. Arterial system carries blood out, venous system brings it back; hepatic portal system (intestine to liver) and renal portal system (lower body to kidney). Blood = plasma + nucleated RBCs with haemoglobin + WBCs + platelets; lymph lacks a few proteins and RBCs.

Respiratory: in water, the skin (cutaneous respiration by diffusion); on land, the buccal cavity, skin and lungs (pulmonary respiration); lungs are a pair of elongated pink sac-like structures in the upper trunk; air enters via nostrils into the buccal cavity and then the lungs; during aestivation and hibernation exchange is through the skin.

Excretory: a pair of compact, dark red, bean-like kidneys on either side of the vertebral column, made of nephrons; ureters (urinogenital ducts in the male; separate from the oviducts in the female) open into the cloaca; thin-walled urinary bladder ventral to the rectum; the frog excretes urea and is ureotelic.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. In the first weeks of the monsoon, a school pond fills with loud croaking at night. Students find pairs of frogs in which a smaller frog clings tightly to the back of a larger one, and a few days later they see floating masses of jelly-like eggs, followed by tiny swimming larvae with tails. By the end of the season the larvae have grown limbs, lost their tails and left the water.
(i) Which sex is the croaking frog, and which structure produces the sound?
(ii) Name the structure that helps the smaller frog cling to the larger one, and state where it is located.
(iii) What type of fertilisation is shown by the floating eggs, and approximately how many ova does a female lay at a time?
(iv) Name the larva and the process by which it becomes an adult.
pyq.answer:
(i) The croaking frog is the male; the sound is produced by the vocal sacs, which are present only in males.
(ii) The copulatory pad, present on the first digit of the forelimbs of the male, helps it grip the female during amplexus.
(iii) External fertilisation in water; a mature female lays 2500 to 3000 ova at a time.
(iv) The larva is the tadpole; it becomes the adult by metamorphosis.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. During a demonstration dissection, a teacher shows students the frog's heart, which keeps beating for a while even after removal, and points out a triangular chamber behind the right atrium, a sac-like tube leaving the ventricle, two bean-shaped dark red organs on either side of the backbone, and a coiled tube from the mouth that is surprisingly short for the size of the animal. Under a microscope the blood shows oval red cells, each with a nucleus.
(i) Name the triangular chamber and the sac-like tube, and state what each does.
(ii) How many chambers does the frog's heart have? Why does it keep beating after removal?
(iii) Name the bean-shaped organs and the nitrogenous waste they remove.
(iv) Why is the alimentary canal short, and how do the frog's RBCs differ from human RBCs?
pyq.answer:
(i) The triangular chamber is the sinus venosus, which joins the right atrium and receives blood from the venae cavae; the sac-like tube is the conus arteriosus, into which the ventricle opens and which carries blood to the arteries.
(ii) Three chambers: two atria and one ventricle. The heart is myogenic and auto-excitable, so it generates its own impulse and keeps beating for some time outside the body.
(iii) The kidneys; they remove urea, so the frog is ureotelic.
(iv) The canal is short because the frog is a carnivore, which reduces the length of the intestine. Frog RBCs are nucleated; human RBCs lose their nucleus.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A farmer notices that frogs disappear from his fields during the hottest weeks of May and again in the coldest weeks of January, and reappear when the weather turns mild. He also observes that a frog sitting on grass looks greener than the same frog sitting on dry soil, and that frogs in his fields keep the insect population low.
(i) Name the two periods of disappearance and state where the frog spends them.
(ii) How does the frog obtain oxygen during these periods?
(iii) What is the colour change called in NCERT, and what is its purpose?
(iv) Give two ways in which frogs are beneficial to the farmer and to the ecosystem.
pyq.answer:
(i) Aestivation (summer sleep) in May and hibernation (winter sleep) in January; both are spent in deep burrows that protect the frog from extreme heat and cold.
(ii) By cutaneous respiration: gaseous exchange takes place through the moist, vascular skin by diffusion, since the lungs are not used.
(iii) The frog changes colour to hide from enemies (camouflage); NCERT calls this protective coloration mimicry.
(iv) Frogs eat insects and so protect crops; they are an important link in food chains and food webs and thus maintain ecological balance (in some countries their legs are also used as food).

common_mistakes: Giving the frog a neck or a tail. The adult frog's body has only a head and a trunk; the tail belongs to the tadpole and is lost at metamorphosis.
Swapping the digit numbers: it is four digits on the forelimb and five on the hind limb. Writing 5 and 4 loses the mark in an MCQ.
Placing the copulatory pad on the hind limb or on all digits. It is on the first digit of the forelimb of the male only, and it is paired with vocal sacs as the two marks of sexual dimorphism.

Calling the heart four-chambered or five-chambered. It is three-chambered (two atria, one ventricle); sinus venosus and conus arteriosus are accessory chambers and must be named separately, not counted.
Writing that frog RBCs are enucleated like human RBCs. Frog RBCs are nucleated and contain haemoglobin; this is the single most common wrong option.
Confusing the two portal systems. Hepatic portal is intestine to liver; renal portal is lower body to kidney. Students also forget that these are venous connections, not arteries.
Saying bile digests fat. Bile emulsifies fat; it contains no enzymes. Pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins.
Reversing aestivation and hibernation, or saying the frog uses its lungs during them. Aestivation is summer, hibernation is winter, and in both the skin alone does the gas exchange.

Attaching the ovaries to the kidneys or giving the female a urinogenital duct. Ovaries have no functional connection with the kidneys, and the oviducts open into the cloaca separately from the ureters; only the male ureter is a urinogenital duct.
Writing the sperm route without the kidney: sperms go testis to vasa efferentia to kidney to Bidder's canal to urinogenital duct to cloaca. Leaving out the kidney or Bidder's canal is marked wrong.
Leaving diagrams unlabelled or labelling in non-NCERT words (for example 'ear' instead of 'tympanum', 'food pipe' instead of 'oesophagus'). Biology marking schemes award marks per correct label.
strategy:
This is a short chapter with a heavy diagram load, so prepare it in three passes over two or three days. Pass one (reading, one sitting): read the NCERT anatomy paragraphs slowly and underline every number and every named structure: three chambers, ten pairs of cranial nerves, 10 to 12 vasa efferentia, 2500 to 3000 ova, eight endocrine glands, five sense organs. Turn each system into a one-line chain with arrows (the formula sheet above is exactly that) and say the chains aloud until the order is automatic.

Pass two (drawing, the longest): draw the four NCERT figures, external features, digestive system, male and female reproductive systems, from memory, then check against the book and redraw whatever you mislabelled. Add the heart and the brain in dorsal view, because they are asked as 3-mark descriptions where a small labelled sketch earns credit. Practise the digestive system until you can produce it, fully labelled, in under five minutes; it is the most probable 5-marker.

Pass three (questions): write out the six 2-mark questions in the pyq section (ureters, aestivation versus hibernation, male versus female, digestive glands, portal systems, brain parts) and the four 3-mark system descriptions, timing yourself at one minute per mark. Then do all the MCQs; each wrong answer is a fact to put back into pass one.

What to memorise: the numbers, the names of glands and sense organs, the colour of the skin and the kidneys, and NCERT's own phrases (poikilotherm, mimicry, urinogenital duct, ureotelic). What to reason: why the canal is short, why the male ureter is urinogenital, why the skin can respire, why the heart beats outside the body. In the exam, answer diagram questions first while your hand is steady, and write anatomy answers as labelled sequences rather than paragraphs; the marking scheme is a list of points and the examiner ticks them.

If you are also preparing for NEET, add the tissue section at the end of this guide and read the older NCERT text on animal tissues once; a question a year still comes from it.
